title: Nachiketa's chariot
hookLine: a boy sent to Death waits three nights at the door, and Death teaches him with a chariot
carry: atman is the rider, not the horses

lines: TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?
cards: A father is giving away his cows at a great sacrifice, and his young son Nachiketa notices they're old ones, past giving milk. So the boy asks: and to whom will you give me? He asks a second time.
A third. And his father, fed up, snaps: to Death. The boy takes him at his word.
He goes to the house of Yama, Death himself, and Yama isn't home. Nachiketa waits at the door for three nights, with nothing to eat.

teach.h: THREE WISHES. WHAT COMES AFTER DEATH?
teach.b: This is the Katha Upanishad. Yama comes home, troubled that a guest has gone hungry, and offers three wishes, one for each night. For the third, the boy asks what everyone avoids: what happens to a person after death?
Yama tries to buy him off. Take sons, gold, horses, a long life.
Nachiketa says: keep your horses. So Death teaches him, and one of his pictures is a chariot. Know the self, the atman, as the one riding in the chariot.
The body is the chariot. The intellect is the driver. The mind is the reins.
The senses are the horses. Here's the big teaching: you are not your restless senses, and not even your racing mind.
In the Upanishads the atman is the true self, the one who rides, and Yama says it is not born and does not die.
When the driver is careless, the senses run wild like bad horses; when the driver understands and the reins are steady, the chariot reaches the end of the road.

Another Upanishad, the Shvetashvatara, carries the chariot straight into breath practice: sit in a clean, level place out of the wind, hold the chest, neck and head upright, let the breath out gently through the nose, and hold the mind the way a driver holds restless horses.
That's an order for a Hindu breath practice, read this way: place, body, breath, mind, so the rider can remember who's riding.

how: Some Hindus who keep a daily breath practice begin by choosing a clean, quiet spot and settling the body upright, in the order the Shvetashvatara Upanishad sets out, and hold the Katha Upanishad's picture of the self as the rider of the chariot.

o: a breathing drill done anywhere, the harder the better
the mind as the true self, steering everything
the self as the rider; body the chariot, senses the horses

s: in the Katha Upanishad, your mind is your true self
the mind is the reins. the atman, the self, is the one riding.
Nachiketa turned down wealth and long life to hear Death's answer
Yama offered sons, gold, horses and long years; the boy kept his question.
the Shvetashvatara Upanishad says to breathe out as hard as you can
it says to let the breath out gently through the nostrils, with the body upright.

games.q: you sit for breath practice and your mind bolts to a fight you had today. in Yama's chariot, who are you?
o: the rider; the horses bolted, but a clear head can gather the reins again.
the horse: the mind is the real you, so follow it.
the road: you go wherever the horses run.
games.why: in the Katha Upanishad the atman rides; the intellect drives, the mind is the reins and the senses the horses. let the driver gather the reins, gently.

practice: Look at where you are, and move one thing that's in the way, a bag, a cup, a buzzing phone. Let the chest, neck and head stack upright, the chariot steady, and let each out-breath leave gently through the nose.
When the mind pulls toward a sound or a worry, picture the reins and bring it back with a light hand; you're the one riding, not the horse that bolted.

wordCard.voice: Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the Upanishads' order and its reason: place, body, breath, mind, because the self, the atman, is the rider.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: atman, the self; in the Katha Upanishad, the one riding in the chariot.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: atman is the rider, not the horses. Nachiketa turned down Death's horses to learn that. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1 (Nachiketa and the three wishes), 1.2.18, 1.3.3–1.3.6
